Understand
ŭn-dər-stănd'
v. (to comprehend, perceive the meaning of; rendering Hebrew bin, sakal, Greek syniemi, noeo)
From Saxon understandan, literally to stand under or among — and the etymology is unusually apt, since Scripture makes understanding a posture beneath the Word rather than a mastery over it.

Biblical Definition

Understanding in Scripture is a gift before it is an achievement, and the Bible is candid about why it must be. Paul's indictment leaves no exception: “There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God” (Romans 3:11). That is not a comment on intelligence; the men in view are as clever as any. The failure is moral and the organ is darkened, so the reversal must come from outside. Luke reports it happening: “Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures” (Luke 24:45). The risen Christ does not merely explain the text to the disciples — He opens the faculty, and only then does the exposition land. The Psalmist therefore asks rather than assumes, and ties the request to obedience: “Give me understanding, and I shall keep thy law; yea, I shall observe it with my whole heart” (Psalm 119:34). Understanding is sought in order to keep, which rules out the notion of a comprehension that leaves conduct untouched. And Nehemiah shows the ordinary means God uses: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Nehemiah 8:8). Read clearly, explained, applied — the pattern of preaching, and the reason the church has ministers. The sovereign opening of Luke 24 and the plain teaching of Nehemiah 8 are not rivals; the second is how the first usually arrives.

Webster 1828 Definition

To comprehend; to have just and adequate ideas of. Scripture holds both that none understands by nature (Romans 3:11) and that Christ opens the understanding (Luke 24:45), with reading and exposition as the ordinary means (Nehemiah 8:8).

expand to see more

UNDERSTAND, v.t. [Sax. understandan; under and standan, to stand.] To have just and adequate ideas of; to comprehend; to know; as, to understand a problem.

2. To have the same ideas as the person who speaks, or the ideas which a speaker intends to communicate. I understand the preacher.

3. To receive or comprehend the meaning of a writing or discourse. They gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading. Neh. 8.

4. To suppose to mean; to interpret; as, in what sense are we to understand this passage?

5. To learn; to be informed. Understanding, n. the faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends the real state of things presented to it. Then opened he their understanding. Luke 24.

Key Scripture

Romans 3:11 — "There is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God."

Luke 24:45 — "Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,"

Psalm 119:34 — "Give me understanding, and I shall keep thy law; yea, I shall observe it with my whole heart."

Nehemiah 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Modern Corruption

Understanding has been relocated from the text to the reader — what a passage means becomes what it means to me — which quietly makes every reading equally valid and therefore makes correction impossible.

expand to see more

The move is often made in a devotional key and sounds humble: who am I to say what it means? But the effect is the opposite of humility. If meaning is supplied by the reader, then the text can never rebuke him, because it can never say anything he did not already put there. Nehemiah 8:8 assumes the contrary at every point. The Levites read distinctly — the words have a fixed shape; they gave the sense — there is a sense to give; they caused them to understand — understanding can be conveyed from one person to another, which is impossible if it is private by nature. The people then wept, which is what happens when a text you did not author tells you something about yourself.

The opposite failure is rationalism, and Romans 3:11 forecloses it just as firmly. The natural man does not lack data; he lacks the faculty, and no amount of scholarship repairs a darkened understanding. This is why Luke 24:45 is such a relief. Christ opened their understanding, and the men whose eyes He opened had walked with Him for three years and still not seen it. Understanding is therefore something to be prayed for before it is studied for, which is exactly the order of Psalm 119:34 — give me understanding, and then I shall keep. A reader who prays that prayer honestly has already surrendered the modern premise, because he has admitted that the meaning is out there, that it is not in his gift, and that when it comes he intends to obey it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew bin (to discern, understand) and its noun binah, with sakal (to be prudent, act wisely); Greek syniemi (to put together, comprehend), synesis (understanding), and noeo (to perceive with the mind).

expand to see more

Hebrew bin (H995) — to separate mentally, discern, understand; the verb behind Nehemiah 8:8 and the Psalmist's plea for understanding.

Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, discernment; paired with wisdom throughout Proverbs and asked for rather than assumed.

Hebrew sakal (H7919) — to be prudent, have insight, act wisely; understanding shown in conduct rather than in speech alone.

Greek syniemi (G4920) — to bring together, and so to comprehend; the word negated in Romans 3:11, “none that understandeth.”

Greek dianoia (G1271) — the mind, the understanding as a faculty; the organ Christ opened in Luke 24:45.

Usage

"“There is none that understandeth” — the failure is moral, not intellectual."

"“Then opened he their understanding” — the faculty opened first, and then the scriptures land."

"“Gave the sense, and caused them to understand” — the pattern of preaching, and the reason for a ministry."
